I disagree, my friend. You say that Mel Gibson was an eighties action star, but that's not exactly accurate. While it's true that the Lethal Weapon (1987) and Mad Max (1979) franchises were probably what elevated him to the Hollywood "A list" and the majority of both series came out in the eighties, those aren't what defined his career. If you look at his adjusted top grossing films you will find that only one from the eighties is in the top ten -- six are from the nineties and his highest all time grossing film was Signs in '02. Look through the list a little further and you will see that he was the biggest draw at the theater in the late nineties and early aughts.

I would argue that his numbers began to taper off in the early two thousands, initially, because he began focusing on directing, with The Passion of the Christ in '04 and Apocalypto in '06. Of course, The Passion is the highest grossing R rated feature ever, and Apocalypto did pretty good with a budget of $40 million and a world-wide gross of $120 million. This was also the beginning of the end for Gibson, as rumors of his anti-semitism began surfacing before The Passion was released; his anti-semitism was laid bare as he ranted about Jews being "responsible for all the wars in the world" during his arrest for DUI in '06; and the nuclear, career ending phone call in 2010, where Gibson unleashed an over the top slur-laden, racist, misogynist rant upon his then lover Oksana Grigorieva(this video is just part 1 of 7).

This is probably stuff that most people know, but I went a little deeper into detail with all of that to illustrate that calling Mel Gibson an "80's action star" is not accurate because the 80's wasn't his defining decade and he wasn't strictly an action star. Edge of Darkness came out in 2010 and it was clear that Mel's controversial few years had essentially ruined his career, the film barely broke even, and this was six months before the recordings were released.

Furthermore, calling Tom Cruise a “90's action star” is also inaccurate. Cruise's two highest adjusted grossing movies are from the 80's and after Top Gun in '86 he has consistently been a box office draw. His movies still bring in the big bucks, but, as the article suggests, after “the couch” he isn't quite seen in the same heavenly light. Closing thoughts on this: he was a big star in the nineties – and the aughts, and the current decade. He also isn't an “action star,” I estimate that about about two thirds of his films aren't action.

I would also say that your comment about Scientology “backing him up,” has little to nothing to do with Tom Cruise's success. He's a big star because, as the article points out, casting Tom Cruise is insurance that your movie wont flop, and these big Hollywood productions are all about making money.

To wrap up, comparing Mel Gibson and Tom Cruise is perfectly valid, and not as you put “quite a different situation.” They are awesome actors that put asses in the seats. Not good actors like Daniel Day Lewis or Phillip Seymour Hoffman, but actors that have mass appeal and were all-time apex “A list” celebrities in their prime.
